name: Ebstein anomaly
aliases: Ebstein malformation of the tricuspid valve

reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: The septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets are displaced apically into the right ventricle, so part of the ventricle becomes incorporated into the right atrium as an atrialised chamber
The malformed valve is usually regurgitant, and the functional right ventricle is small and often poorly contractile
Severity is highly variable, from a critically cyanotic neonate to an incidental finding in an adult
An atrial-level communication is common and allows right-to-left shunting with cyanosis, especially when right heart pressures are high
There is a well-recognised association with accessory pathways and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, predisposing to tachyarrhythmias
Neonatal presentation can be severe because high pulmonary resistance worsens tricuspid regurgitation and cyanosis, improving as resistance falls
Management ranges from observation to arrhythmia ablation and surgical tricuspid repair or reconstruction (cone repair) depending on severity
reference.pathophysiology: In Ebstein anomaly the tricuspid valve leaflets fail to delaminate normally from the right ventricular wall, so the septal and posterior leaflets are displaced towards the apex. This incorporates the inflow portion of the right ventricle into the right atrium as a thin, poorly contractile atrialised segment, leaving a reduced functional right ventricle. The abnormal valve is typically regurgitant, and the combination of tricuspid regurgitation, a large functionally impaired right atrium and a small right ventricle limits forward pulmonary flow. When right atrial pressure exceeds left, blood shunts right to left across an associated atrial communication, producing cyanosis. Disordered conduction tissue and accessory atrioventricular pathways underlie the frequent association with pre-excitation and reentrant tachyarrhythmias.
additionalDifferentials: Right atrial enlargement from other causes
Uhl anomaly and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum
Pericardial effusion causing an enlarged cardiac silhouette
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to measure leaflet displacement, quantify regurgitation and assess right ventricular function
Electrocardiogram for pre-excitation, right atrial enlargement and conduction abnormalities
Cardiac MRI to assess right ventricular volumes and the atrialised segment
Electrophysiological study when accessory pathways or tachyarrhythmias are suspected
Chest radiograph, which may show marked cardiomegaly with a globular heart
Assessment of an atrial-level shunt and its direction
redFlags: Severe neonatal cyanosis with a massively enlarged heart and low output
Symptomatic tachyarrhythmia, particularly with an accessory pathway
Progressive right heart failure from severe tricuspid regurgitation
Syncope or haemodynamic collapse during arrhythmia
reference.prognosis: Outcome spans a wide range: mild disease is compatible with a normal life, while severe neonatal presentations carry high mortality; arrhythmias add risk, and modern tricuspid repair offers durable improvement in selected patients.
pitfalls: Underestimating the arrhythmia risk from an associated accessory pathway
Misinterpreting neonatal cyanosis that may improve as pulmonary resistance falls and prompting premature intervention
Confusing the atrialised right ventricle with global right ventricular dilatation of other cause
Overlooking a right-to-left atrial shunt as the source of cyanosis and paradoxical embolism
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
